questions.prompt: A hiker is bitten by a rabid raccoon. The raccoon is the reservoir, which makes rabies a:
questions.explanation: Zoonoses move from animals to humans.

questions.prompt: Children in a daycare pass a stomach virus by sharing toys. This is:
questions.explanation: A fomite is a non-living object that serves as the middleman.

questions.prompt: A coworker sneezes on you from about half a meter away. This transmission is:
questions.explanation: Droplet = less than 1 meter; airborne (vehicle) = more than 1 meter.

questions.prompt: Which statement about vectors is FALSE?

options.text: The Anopheles mosquito is a biological vector for malaria.
In a biological vector, the pathogen reproduces inside the arthropod.
A mechanical vector carries pathogens on its body parts.
A housefly is a biological vector because Plasmodium reproduces in it.
Vectors are living; vehicles are not.

questions.explanation: The housefly is a mechanical vector; the mosquito is the biological vector for Plasmodium.

questions.prompt: Which portal of entry is used by most pathogens?
questions.explanation: Mucous membranes exchange materials with the outside world and are the most vulnerable.

questions.prompt: Stepping on a rusty nail deposits bacteria beneath intact skin. This portal is the:
questions.explanation: Parenteral = something plunges through intact skin.

questions.prompt: Give three reasons healthcare facilities are sources of HAIs, and three ways to prevent them.
questions.explanation: Reasons: many reservoirs (sick patients), many invasive procedures (catheters, surgery, dressing changes), many compromised hosts. Prevention: hand washing, PPE, aseptic technique, isolation, education.

questions.prompt: Why are catheters such a common cause of UTIs in hospitals?

options.text: Bacteria form biofilms on catheters left in too long
Catheters release toxins into the bladder wall
Catheters lower the pH of urine to about 2
Catheters destroy the IgA antibodies in urine

questions.explanation: UTIs are the most common HAI, and catheter biofilms are the main culprit.

questions.prompt: Streptococcus pyogenes holds onto throat tissue and resists phagocytosis using:
questions.explanation: M-protein does double duty: adherence and inhibiting phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: Encapsulated strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae cause pneumonia but unencapsulated strains are mostly harmless. Why?
questions.explanation: White blood cells struggle to engulf the slippery encapsulated cells.

questions.prompt: Which statement about coagulase and kinase is FALSE?

options.text: Kinase clots blood so the pathogen can hide from white blood cells.
Coagulase builds a clot barricade around the infection.
Kinase helps a pathogen escape a clot made by the host.

questions.explanation: Coagulase clots blood; kinase digests clots.

questions.prompt: Yersinia pestis damages the host by producing substances that pull iron out of red blood cells. These are:
questions.explanation: Siderophores bind host nutrients like iron extremely strongly.

questions.prompt: Clostridium perfringens causes gangrene mainly by producing:
questions.explanation: Digesting connective tissue (including blood vessels) kills the tissue.

questions.prompt: Émile Roux's first diphtheria filtrates didn't harm guinea pigs. What changed to make the experiment work?

options.text: He let the culture grow about two weeks before filtering
He stopped filtering and injected the whole culture
He heated the filtrate to concentrate the toxin
He switched from guinea pigs to mice for the tests

questions.explanation: At 24–48 hours the bacteria hadn't released enough toxin yet.

questions.prompt: Botox comes from a Type III (A-B) exotoxin of Clostridium botulinum. How does it work?

options.text: It blocks signals from neurons to muscles, causing paralysis
It lyses red blood cells in the injected muscle
It causes an excessive immune response in the skin
It steals iron from muscle cells so they can't contract

questions.explanation: It's a neurotoxin; the body slowly breaks it down, so injections are repeated.

questions.prompt: Compare exotoxins and endotoxins: what they're made of, which bacteria make them, and when they're released.
questions.explanation: Exotoxins are proteins secreted mostly by Gram-positive bacteria (often encoded by prophage genes from lysogenic conversion); types are superantigens, hemolysins, and A-B toxins. Endotoxins are part of the Gram-negative cell wall (LPS) and are released when the cell dies and breaks apart, causing excessive immune responses.
